distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for the full clinical spectrum of secondary syphilis.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Spirochetes disseminate from the inoculation site through blood and lymphatics, producing a systemic infectious stage with high organism burden in skin, mucosa, lymphoid tissue, and sometimes liver, kidney, eye, CNS, or ear.
Host inflammatory response to disseminated spirochetes produces fever, malaise, fatigue, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, anorexia, and mild acute-phase reactant elevation.

Dense treponemal infiltration and plasma-cell-rich inflammation in skin and mucosa produce the polymorphic rash, palmoplantar lesions, mucous patches, condyloma lata, patchy alopecia, and occasionally nodular or ulceronecrotic lesions.
Antigenic stimulation and tissue dissemination drive generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and mild hematologic or inflammatory laboratory changes.

Treponemal dissemination and periportal inflammatory injury can produce disproportionate alkaline phosphatase elevation, mild to moderate AST/ALT elevation, abdominal symptoms, and rare clinically significant hepatitis.
Circulating treponemal antigen-antibody complexes can deposit in glomeruli and produce proteinuria, membranous-pattern nephropathy, edema, hypoalbuminemia, and rare nephrotic syndrome.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Ocular, CNS, and otic inflammatory seeding
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Disseminated infection can involve uveal tract, retina, optic nerve, meninges, cranial nerves, or inner ear during secondary-stage disease, causing panuveitis, visual symptoms, meningitis-like symptoms, or otosyphilis.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Disseminated organism burden is the upstream driver of constitutional inflammatory symptoms.
Skin and mucosal lesions contain abundant organisms and often dominate the clinical phenotype.
Systemic antigenic stimulation explains generalized lymph node and reticuloendothelial involvement.
Hepatic involvement is a recognized systemic manifestation of secondary-stage disease.
Antigen load and host antibody response can form immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli.
Ocular, neurologic, and otic involvement can occur during early disseminated syphilis.
Fever is common but may be absent at a single visit.
Several days to weeks of intermittent fever may precede or accompany the rash.
Constitutional symptoms are part of the systemic secondary-stage syndrome.
Myalgia often accompanies fever and malaise.
Headache can reflect systemic inflammation or early meningeal involvement.
The rash is the dominant clinically recognized secondary syphilis manifestation.
Macules and papules are common morphologies, though secondary syphilis is polymorphic.
Palm and sole involvement is a highly useful ordinary clinical clue but can be absent.
Oral and genital mucous patches are spirochete-rich secondary lesions.
Moist intertriginous papules and plaques represent infectious mucocutaneous secondary lesions.
Ulceronodular and necrotic lesions are uncommon but real secondary-stage presentations.
Moth-eaten patchy alopecia is a recognized secondary syphilis manifestation.
Generalized painless lymphadenopathy is a common systemic finding.
The extent and activity of lymphadenopathy track lymphoid activation.
Syphilitic hepatitis often has a cholestatic or mixed pattern with disproportionate alkaline phosphatase elevation.
AST can rise mildly or moderately with hepatic involvement.
ALT can rise mildly or moderately with hepatic involvement.
Clinically significant hepatitis is an uncommon but outcome-relevant secondary syphilis complication.
Immune-complex nephropathy presents first as proteinuria.
Nephrotic-range proteinuria can occur in syphilitic membranous nephropathy.
Heavy urinary protein loss lowers serum albumin when nephrotic syndrome develops.
Proteinuria, edema, and hypoalbuminemia define the clinically important renal event.
Anterior uveitis can be part of syphilitic panuveitis.
Posterior uveitis, retinitis, vasculitis, and panuveitis are important ocular syphilis patterns.
Floaters, flashers, blurred vision, and decreased acuity reflect ocular involvement.
Ocular involvement is a treatment-changing event because it threatens vision and changes the required antibiotic exposure.
Meningitis or cranial nerve involvement can overlap with secondary-stage disease.
Sensorineural hearing or vestibular involvement can occur in early syphilis and changes treatment urgency.

Any secondary syphilis-compatible rash; morphology can be macular, papular, papulosquamous, annular, nodular, pustular, or ulceronecrotic.

Hazard of persistent or rising nontreponemal titers from reinfection, inadequate exposure, nonadherence, or unrecognized CNS/ocular disease.

Disease-specific lifespan hazard from secondary syphilis itself; generally very low, rising mainly with severe CNS involvement, extreme Jarisch-Herxheimer physiology, severe hepatitis, nephrotic complications, or major comorbidity.
Qualitative positive nontreponemal RPR or VDRL when numeric titer is unavailable. This is confirmatory evidence; case files should mark it use_in_ranking:false.
Quantitative nontreponemal RPR or VDRL titer. This is confirmatory and monitoring evidence; case files should mark it use_in_ranking:false.
Treponemal antibody, TPPA, TPHA, FTA-ABS, EIA, or related treponemal test positivity. This is confirmatory evidence and should not be ordinary ranking evidence.

Skin biopsy pattern supportive of secondary syphilis such as plasma-cell-rich dermatitis, granulomatous inflammation, pustular change, or compatible perivascular dermatitis when direct organism detection is not reported. Confirmatory/context pathology; mark use_in_ranking:false in cases.
Histology, immunohistochemistry, or special stain showing treponemal organisms in a skin lesion. Confirmatory pathology; mark use_in_ranking:false in cases.
Treponema pallidum PCR positivity from lesion material. Confirmatory pathogen evidence; mark use_in_ranking:false in cases.
CSF VDRL positivity in suspected neurosyphilis. Confirmatory/contextual evidence and should not be ordinary first-pass ranking evidence.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Only when fever is active near the snapshot; many patients are afebrile at evaluation.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: A febrile prodrome and measured fever are related but not interchangeable.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Palmoplantar involvement is common but not required.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Diffuse secondary rash often includes acral surfaces.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Highest when mucous patches, condyloma lata, or moist skin lesions are present.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Secondary mucocutaneous lesions are infectious and drive onward transmission hazard.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Applies to exposed mucosal contact before effective treatment.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Syphilitic hepatitis often creates a mixed but cholestatic-skewed liver enzyme pattern.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Stronger when viral, obstructive, autoimmune, and medication causes are less likely.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Disproportionate cholestatic enzyme elevation is a key ordinary signal of clinically meaningful hepatic involvement.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Only when a quantified 24-hour urine protein is available.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: The activity score and measurement encode the same renal process at different granularity.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Applies when proteinuria is sustained or nephrotic range.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Heavy urinary protein loss lowers serum albumin over time.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Stronger when serum albumin is low.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Nephrotic protein loss produces edema through reduced oncotic pressure.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Higher logMAR means worse visual acuity.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Posterior inflammation and panuveitis can reduce visual acuity.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Ocular syphilis can be asymptomatic early but usually becomes symptomatic when inflammation is clinically significant.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: The ocular event manifests as visual symptoms and uveitis.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Mortality remains low in treated disease but rises with severe CNS involvement or major comorbidity.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: CNS disease is the main lifespan-relevant secondary-stage complication.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Mainly relevant if hepatitis is severe, delayed, or occurs on limited hepatic reserve.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Secondary syphilitic hepatitis is usually reversible but can add risk in severe presentations.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Relevant when nephrotic syndrome is severe, thrombotic, infected, or superimposed on renal/cardiovascular disease.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Nephrotic syndrome is rarely fatal by itself but can increase complication risk.
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction causes an acute fever and systemic inflammatory spike.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Mostly relevant in pregnancy, cardiovascular frailty, severe systemic disease, or hypotensive reaction.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: The reaction is usually self-limited but can be outcome-relevant in vulnerable contexts.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Maternal lifespan hazard is not the main concern; this coupling only captures rare severe obstetric/systemic consequences.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy primarily changes fetal outcome and treatment urgency rather than maternal mortality.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: True immediate penicillin allergy changes the usable pathway; pregnancy or neuro/ocular disease favors desensitization rather than nonpenicillin substitution.
Ocular disease requires sustained IV aqueous penicillin exposure rather than relying on single-dose benzathine penicillin alone.
Symptomatic CNS involvement requires neurosyphilis therapy.

failure_modes: incorrect stage or unrecognized ocular/CNS/otic disease requiring a different exposure profile
reinfection from untreated partner
missed diagnosis of another rash illness or coinfection
true penicillin allergy without desensitization plan

side_effects.interpretation: Acute post-treatment inflammatory reaction from treponemal lysis.
Transient fever spike during Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

treatments.context_specific_role: Treponemicidal therapy for secondary-stage disease without ocular, otic, or neurologic organ-event context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Sustained IV exposure is needed when syphilis threatens ocular structures.
CNS involvement requires adequate CSF exposure.
No equally proven nonpenicillin regimen exists for pregnancy or neurosyphilis-style disease.

failure_modes: delayed ophthalmology or neurology recognition before irreversible injury
premature discontinuation of IV course
coinfection or non-syphilitic ocular inflammatory disease

side_effects.interpretation: Post-treatment inflammatory reaction can occur after IV therapy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Treponemicidal exposure path for ocular, CNS, or otic organ-event phenotypes.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and does not reliably prevent fetal infection.
Ocular disease needs neurosyphilis-style therapy rather than oral doxycycline alone.
Oral doxycycline is not a robust pathway for symptomatic CNS disease.

failure_modes: missed doses or incomplete course
use in pregnancy
unrecognized ocular, otic, or CNS disease
reinfection before partner treatment

side_effects.interpretation: Photosensitivity or drug eruption can confuse rash tracking.

treatments.context_specific_role: Nonpregnant oral alternative pathway when penicillin cannot be used and reliable follow-up/adherence are available.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Evidence is insufficient for preventing congenital syphilis compared with penicillin.
Cephalosporin cross-reactivity is low but not zero; allergy details matter.

failure_modes: uncertain optimal dose or duration for uncomplicated secondary-stage disease
use when penicillin desensitization is needed for pregnancy or CNS/ocular certainty
loss to follow-up after nonpenicillin regimen
treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral alternative path when penicillin cannot be used immediately and specialist follow-up is reliable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Desensitization is only relevant when a true penicillin allergy blocks the otherwise necessary penicillin pathway.
Pregnancy removes proven nonpenicillin alternatives and raises fetal-event stakes.

failure_modes: desensitization performed without monitored setting when high-risk allergy exists
interruption after desensitization before penicillin course is completed
misclassified non-allergic adverse reaction causing unnecessary delay

side_effects.interpretation: Breakthrough allergic symptoms can occur during desensitization.

treatments.context_specific_role: Context-enabling pathway that permits penicillin treatment when allergy would otherwise block the needed regimen.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ocular inflammation control does not eradicate Treponema pallidum and should not replace treponemicidal therapy.

failure_modes: anti-inflammatory treatment without treponemicidal therapy
intraocular pressure rise
missed posterior segment disease requiring systemic management

side_effects.interpretation: Steroid-associated intraocular pressure or cataract effects can worsen visual complaints over time.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunctive ocular symptom and inflammation control when ophthalmology documents uveitis.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior probability of acquired syphilis and other STI coinfections; does not by itself determine disease severity.
Can increase prior probability, atypical or severe cutaneous phenotypes, ocular/CNS involvement concern, and serologic follow-up complexity.
Maternal disease likelihood is not intrinsically higher, but fetal-event hazard and treatment constraints dominate management.
Does not change disease biology but changes treatment path and failure/toxicity risk.
Prolongs active disease, raises organ-event and serologic failure hazards, and increases need to distinguish reinfection from treatment failure.
Does not cause secondary syphilis, but makes hepatic or renal involvement more outcome-relevant and harder to attribute.

supportive_care.clinical_role: Assess pregnancy and coexisting STI/HIV context, counsel abstinence until treatment and lesion resolution, and arrange partner notification/evaluation/treatment to reduce reinfection and transmission.

Use RPR/VDRL and treponemal tests for diagnosis confirmation and response monitoring; these axes are confirmatory evidence and should not be consumed as ordinary presentation likelihood in case ranking.
Urgent ophthalmology, audiology, neurology, lumbar puncture, and IV therapy pathway when visual, auditory, or neurologic symptoms are present.
Antipyretics, hydration, observation, and obstetric monitoring when needed; do not delay necessary treponemicidal therapy solely because of reaction risk.
Evaluate alternative viral, autoimmune, obstructive, medication, diabetic, and primary renal causes while treating syphilis when ordinary clinical syndrome supports it.
Topical steroids, cycloplegics, and follow-up visual assessment can reduce ocular inflammation but must accompany treponemicidal therapy.

quality_warnings: Disease-specific prompt scope is only Disease: Secondary syphilis (id: D-SECONDARY-SYPHILIS); HIV, ocular disease, malignant morphology, pregnancy, and organ complications are context or phenotype axes, not disease-name qualifiers.
RPR, VDRL, treponemal serology, PCR, and biopsy organism detection are confirmatory axes for ontology completeness; case files should place them in confirmatory_findings with use_in_ranking:false.
Only mortality_hazard_in_D-SECONDARY-SYPHILIS is category derived_hazard; organ events and treatment reactions are event_hazard axes.
